title: Liking things
description: Say what you like, and what you do not.

explanation.summary: Spanish says what you like with gustar, and the thing you like comes first. This is the opposite of English, and it is the first real difference a learner has to unlearn.

sections.heading: The order is reversed
sections.body: Me gusta el café says the coffee is pleasing to me. The coffee is the subject, and the person is a me, te, le, nos at the front. If more than one thing is liked, it becomes plural: me gustan las pizzas. So you say me gusta for one thing, and me gustan for several.

examples.es: A mi hermana le gusta el fútbol.

sections.heading: Stronger and softer
sections.body: Gustar is to like. Encantar is to love, and it works the same way: me encanta el chocolate. To say you do not like something, you put no in front and keep the order: no me gusta el pescado. And to say something is boring, use aburrir: la película es aburrida.

sections.heading: There is, and there is not
sections.body: Hay says there is, and it never changes: hay un banco, hay dos bancos, no hay bancos. The verb is always hay, whatever the number.

examples.es: Hay un parque cerca de la plaza.
examples.en: There is a park near the square.

examples.es: No hay agua en la nevera.
examples.en: There is no water in the fridge.

exercises.prompt: Pair each word with its translation.
exercises.note: In English the subject comes first: I like coffee. In Spanish the thing comes first: me gusta el café.

exercises.prompt: Pick the Spanish word for “to like”.
exercises.note: An infinitive. Me gusta, te gusta, le gusta: the thing you like comes first.
The person comes first with gustar.
